---
engine: markdown
title: "Report an estimate with its error"
subtitle: "Two columns read as one, because that is how a reader reads them."
description: "Use columns-combine to print an estimate beside its standard error and an interval from its bounds, each as a single column."
---

An estimate and its standard error are one number to a reader, and so are the two bounds of an interval.
`columns-combine` builds one column from several, through a pattern that takes one argument per source.

```{typst}
//| file: ../../tests/visual/combined.typ
//| echo: true
//| alt: "An association table with centred column labels, a gene column, an effect column holding each estimate followed by its standard error in brackets, a confidence interval column holding two bounds joined by a dash, and a p column in scientific notation. In both combined columns, the estimates, errors and bounds line up on their decimal points, and the brackets and dashes line up too."
```

The estimate keeps two decimals and the error three, because the pattern receives the formatted content of its sources rather than their raw values.
That is why `combine` sits after `format` in the pipeline.

Each value still lines up down the column.
The estimates line up on their decimal separators, and so do the errors.
The bracket and the dash between the values line up too.
Keisen finds the values with a second call to the pattern, with markers in place of the sources.
[How a combined column lines up](../reference/columns.qmd#how-a-combined-column-lines-up) gives the rules, and the cases where a cell is not lined up.
A combined column cannot be summarised, because content has no total.

A label follows its own column by default, so these labels would not share one edge.
`column-labels-align` centres every one of them instead, the stubhead included, and leaves the cells where their columns put them.
